newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: BELARUS LEADER TELLS CRITICS NOT TO MEDDLE.
newsitem.headline: BELARUS LEADER TELLS CRITICS NOT TO MEDDLE.

text.p: Western leaders lined up on Monday to attack Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko's record on democracy at a European security summit, but he hit back by warning the rest of the world to mind its own business.

"It would be counterproductive to try to exert pressure on us or try to interfere in our internal affairs," Lukashenko bluntly told the Lisbon meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

Lukashenko, said by his foes to have dictatorial tendencies, attended the two-day meeting of more than 54 nations despite growing criticism that a referendum on November 24 which gave him sweeping powers was neither free nor fair.
Initiating unusually harsh condemnation of one OSCE member state, the organisation's chairman in office, Flavio Cotti, said he was "deeply concerned" with the situation in Belarus.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore, British Prime Minister John Major and President John Bruton of Ireland, which holds the European Union's rotating presidency, also joined the attack.
"The European Union remains profoundly concerned at the constitutional referendum in Belarus and the resulting developments there," Bruton said.
"We call upon Belarus to respect its commitment to OSCE norms and democratic principles.

Leaders of Poland, Ukraine and Lithuania expressed concern after meeting in Lisbon on Sunday to discuss the situation in their neighbouring state. An international human rights group, the Vienna-based Helsinki Federation for Human Rights, called on Monday for Belarus to be suspended from the OSCE.

Completely unruffled, Lukashenko denied there was a political crisis in Belarus, accused the United States of double standards, blasted NATO plans to expand eastwards and told Washington, the OSCE and neighbouring states not to meddle.
"The United States is, of course, a great power but this does not give it the right to interfere in the affairs of another state," Lukashenko told a news conference.
He said he was flattered by the attention of the leaders of Ukraine, Lithuania and Poland, but added sarcastically: "I think there are enough problems in their own countries to deal with."

Lukashenko said the much-criticised referendum had been completely legitimate and democratic, and defended his handling of a crisis in which his opponents in parliament had threatened to try to impeach him.

"The recent referendum held in Belarus was held in full compliance with the constitution and legislation of our country. Any attempt to represent the results as not legitimate are completely without foundation," Lukashenko said.
"I emphasise strongly that we do not have a political crisis and there is no hint of a division in our society, despite what out internal opposition would have you believe."
Belarus's only remaining major ally is Russia, with which the economically struggling country of 10 million is seeking closer integration five years after the Soviet Union's collapse.

In remarks likely to add to the wrath of the rest of Europe, Lukashenko joined Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in condemning NATO's plans to take in other countries of eastern and central Europe.
"When the military machine comes closer to Russia, it will pass through Belarus on the way. Belarus will find itself on the border of two blocs," he told the news conference.
